newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Thousands of new Zairean rebels parade in Goma.
newsitem.headline: Thousands of new Zairean rebels parade in Goma.

text.p: Some 5,000 newly-trained Zairean rebel troops paraded through the streets of Goma on Thursday singing battle songs praising rebel leader Laurent Kabila and denouncing Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko.
Rebel officers said the new recruits would then be dispatched to join their comrades advancing on four fronts against government forces.
The officers said frontline units were about to enter the northeastern town of Isiro where some of the 300 foreign mercenaries hired by Kinshasa to crush the revolt are based.
"The fall of Isiro is a matter of hours," a senior rebel commander told Reuters. Isiro is about 520 km (325 miles) northwest of Goma, which fell to the rebels in early November.
The parade coincided with rebel officers saying frontline units were closing in on mercenaries in the northeastern town of Isiro.
Life came to a standstill in Goma as many of its 300,000 residents lined a 10-km (six-mile) route from the airport to the city centre to cheer the parade of new rebels to be addressed by Kabila.
Dressed in new U.S.-type combat fatigues and wellington boots, the new recruits sang battle songs praising rebel leader Laurent Kabila and denouncing Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko.

Church sources and aid workers said on Thursday rebels had captured the eastern town of Shabunda and were advancing towards Kindu, one of the springboards for a counter-offensive the army launched last month.

The rebels, who frustrated the army offensive by opening up new fronts, were advancing in large numbers towards Kindu, with its army base and airport about 200 km (125 miles) to the west, the sources added from the region.
The sources said Shabunda fell on Wednesday. Up to 40,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees fled westwards into the forest earlier after reports that the rebels had seized a nearby town.
To the north, on the road from the rebel-held east to the strategic town of Kisangani, relief workers spoke of a movement of people from Amisi refugee camp but had no details of why.

An official of Zaire's state-run mineral mining company Gecamines on Thursday said he saw no immediate danger from the rebel advance and hoped a deal would soon be signed with a South African company.

"Everything is very calm here...obviously things may change, but it is much too early to say we will be affected," Technical Director Yumba Monga told Reuters in Nairobi by telephone from Zaire's copper and cobalt mining centre of Lubumbashi.
The rebels have advanced into the southeastern region of Shaba to the port of Kalemie, 800 km (500 miles), northeast of Lubumbashi, and control a 1,000-km (600-mile) long swath of territory.
An official at rebel headquarters in Goma said on Wednesday rebels were advancing on the southeastern town of Mboa and Kabila said government reinforcements arrived there too late.
Kabila's radio station in Goma broadcast an appeal to King Hassan of Morocco requesting him to ignore a request for military aid from Mobutu, who is visiting his longtime ally.
Kabila said he was ready to open up corridors for more than 100,000 Rwandan Hutus trapped around Kisangani and Lubutu and appealed to the U.N. refugee agency to approach him to make arrangements.
The United States said on Wednesday it had urged Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi to stay out of the fighting in east Zaire.

"The United States appeals again to the neighbours of Zaire to stay out of Zaire, to not involve themselves in the fighting," a State Department spokesman said. "We have underscored this message to Uganda and Rwanda and Burundi."
Zaire has accused all three of sending their troops into eastern Zaire to fight alongside the rebels. All three countries, which border on rebel-held territory, deny doing so.
